title: A 45-degree line. A slope of five.
hook: One square up. One square across. Why is the slope five?
first_frame: A line through (0,10) and (4,30), drawn one grid cell up per cell across. x ticks read 0,2,4; y ticks read 10,20,30. Caption: slope = 1?
prior_knowledge: Coordinate axes and change in a quantity.
promise: Read slope in coordinate units, even when the picture tempts you to count squares.
proof_sequence: Trace the two-by-two-cell right triangle already on the line. Attach the endpoint coordinates without changing the grid. Its horizontal change is 4 and vertical change is 20. The quotient 20/4 is 5. Advance x by 2 along the same line: y advances by 10, confirming the ratio.
visual: One persistent graph and one rise/run triangle. Cell counts become unit counts in place; the two axis labels remain visible through division. No corrective zoom or rescaling.
transfer_question: A line passes through (1,4) and (3,10). Slope?
guardrail: A 45-degree line on the page need not have slope 1. Aspect ratio and coordinate units must be explicit.
why_selected: The eye supplies a tempting answer; the labeled units reveal a genuine discrepancy.
alternate_angle: What do the squares actually measure?
evidence_scope: Adaptation: sampled CodeMatrix shape-to-graph correspondence and MVP replacement-diagram construction with all 16 membership cases verified. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified in the reviewed sequence. No reviewed winner demonstrated this slope trap.
revision_reason: Makes the visual misreading available immediately, then preserves exactly the same graph while the units repair it.
main_question: What is the slope of the line through (0,10) and (4,30), with the displayed unequal axis units?
recognition_cue: Whenever graph-axis units differ, read coordinate changes before judging the angle.
output_rejection: Essential tick values are tiny, the scales change during the reveal, or counting cells is presented as a valid slope calculation.

title: The two strips missing from (x + 4)²
hook: These two squares do not fill the square. What is missing?
first_frame: An outlined (x+4)-square is already split at x and 4 in both directions. x² and 16 occupy opposite corners; the two remaining rectangles are blank. Caption: what is missing?
prior_knowledge: Square area and multiplication.
promise: See exactly where the cross term comes from.
proof_sequence: Use the concrete x=3 partition first: a 7-by-7 square contains a 3-by-3 square, a 4-by-4 square and two 3-by-4 rectangles. Name each strip 4x as the x label replaces 3. Add the four regions: x²+4x+4x+16. Collect to x²+8x+16. Distributivity establishes the same identity for all real x.
visual: Do not build a generic title card. Start on the incomplete accounting. The uncounted rectangles gain a blue outline, receive 4x labels and join symbolically; the physical pieces stay fixed.
transfer_question: Expand (x + 2)².
guardrail: Physical side-length picture assumes x >= 0; distributivity extends the identity to every real x. One numerical check only disproves the wrong identity.
why_selected: A familiar error becomes an actual missing region. Strong broad entry and visible proof.
alternate_angle: Why does squaring a sum create three terms?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from a sampled replacement four-set diagram with all 16 membership cases verified, plus geometric factorization. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified. The new binomial lesson is our construction, not a reviewed reference topic.
revision_reason: Moves the actual missing-area question into the first frame and starts with checkable numbers before general notation.
main_question: Expand (x+4)² and explain the middle term.
recognition_cue: Squaring a sum multiplies each part by both parts, so both cross products must appear.
output_rejection: The two strips arrive as decoration after the answer, or negative x is silently treated as a physical length.

title: Remove a square. Reveal two factors.
hook: How does a square minus a square become a rectangle?
first_frame: An 8-by-8 square with its upper-right 3-by-3 corner removed. The remaining L-shape is intact; area = 64-9 = ?.
prior_knowledge: Square and rectangle area, distributivity, and factoring as writing a product.
promise: See the side lengths that create the difference-of-squares factors.
proof_sequence: The remaining area is 64-9=55. Cut vertically below the removed corner: the left piece is 5 wide by 8 high; the lower-right piece is 3 wide by 5 high. Rotate only that 3-by-5 piece to be 5 wide by 3 high and attach it above the left piece. The rectangle is 5 wide by 11 high. Replace 8 by x: its sides are x-3 and x+3. Expand (x-3)(x+3) to verify x²-9 for every real x.
answer: x²-9 = (x-3)(x+3); the opening area is 55 square units.
visual: Preserve both cut pieces without stretching, overlap or gaps. Their shared dimension 5 becomes x-3; stacked dimensions 8 and 3 become x+3. Use the house blue only on the moving piece.
transfer_question: Factor x²-25.
guardrail: The nondegenerate area construction uses x>3. Algebra proves the identity for all real x; x=3 is a zero-area boundary. Rotation preserves each piece, not its displayed orientation.
why_selected: A literal construction earns an algebraic shortcut and gives the batch a removal/reassembly operation distinct from expanding a square.
alternate_angle: Where do x-3 and x+3 physically come from?
evidence_scope: Direct concept analogue: Animathions difference-of-squares sampled visual review, 1,834 views. This was not that channel’s maximum and is not presented as a mega-winner.
revision_reason: New brief: adds a reviewed domain-specific construction rather than another formula-only simplification.
main_question: Factor x²-9. Use x=8 as the opening area example.
recognition_cue: A difference of two squares factors into a difference times a sum.
output_rejection: A piece changes area in transit, labels no longer measure its sides, or the positive-length illustration is claimed as a proof for negative x.

title: 20% off. What was the original price?
hook: Eighty dollars is only eight pieces. What do all ten cost?
first_frame: Ten equal price cells already outlined. Eight hold a visible $80 bracket; two are empty. Labels: after 20% off; original = ?.
prior_knowledge: A percent is a fraction of an identified whole.
promise: Recover an original amount from a discounted amount.
proof_sequence: The original whole is the same ten-cell outline throughout. Eight cells cost $80, so one costs $10. Rebuild the missing two cells: ten cost $100. Translate that reconstruction into 0.8P=80, so P=80/0.8=100. An add-20%-to-$80 attempt reaches only $96 because it uses the wrong base.
answer: $100 original; divide the final price by 0.8.
visual: The full outline stays fixed while missing cells are restored. Brackets explicitly distinguish $80, 80% of original, from the 100% original price.
transfer_question: After 25% off, a bag costs $90. Original?
guardrail: The percentage is relative to the original price. Tax and successive discounts are outside this example.
why_selected: Everyday stakes, an attemptable wrong turn, and a countable reconstruction.
alternate_angle: Why does adding 20% fail to undo 20% off?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled nested reference-whole reasoning and hidden-area accounting. Neither reviewed clip establishes a discount-video performance result.
revision_reason: Opens on the eligible fraction of a fixed whole and earns inverse multiplication through reconstruction.
main_question: A bag costs $80 after a 20% discount. What was its original price?
recognition_cue: If you know a percentage of the original, divide by the retained decimal to recover the original.
output_rejection: The 100% outline silently shrinks to $80 or a 20% increase is drawn as undoing the discount.

title: The root your division erased
hook: Two curves cross twice. Why did your algebra find only five?
first_frame: A coordinate graph shows y=x² and y=5x, with intersections at x=0 and x=5; beside it, x²=5x leads to a tentative x=5.
prior_knowledge: Factoring a common x, the zero-product property, and graph intersections as equal outputs.
promise: Recognize the zero solution that division can discard.
proof_sequence: Touch the crossing at zero and substitute: 0²=5·0. Revisit the division step: x²/x=5x/x assumes x is nonzero, so it omitted that case. Rewrite the original as x(x-5)=0. Branch on the two factors, obtaining 0 and 5. Verify both in the original and keep both graph intersections.
visual: Link every candidate to its actual graph crossing. A small x≠0 condition appears on the division operation; it never pretends to delete the zero point from the original graph.
transfer_question: Solve x² = 7x.
guardrail: Dividing by x is valid only after treating x = 0 separately; do not imply dividing by a variable is always illegal.
why_selected: A correct answer visibly vanishes, giving a precise reason to keep watching.
alternate_angle: What condition did this division assume?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from a sampled replacement four-set diagram with all 16 membership cases verified, plus linked visual correspondences. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified. The specific lost-root lesson is new.
revision_reason: Replaces a purely decorative disappearing dot with two independently inspectable equal-output crossings.
main_question: Solve x²=5x over the real numbers.
recognition_cue: Before dividing by a variable expression, separately test the case where it is zero.
output_rejection: The original graph loses a genuine intersection, factoring is skipped, or the lesson says division by a variable is always forbidden.

title: The apex moves. The area does not.
hook: Slide this corner past the base. Does the area change?
first_frame: A triangle spans base endpoints (0,0),(10,0). Its apex (2,6) sits on a visible horizontal track y=6; an outlined ghost apex at (12,6) suggests the move.
prior_knowledge: Parallelogram area as base times perpendicular height, and triangle duplication.
promise: Recognize why slanted side length does not determine triangle area.
proof_sequence: Keep the same two base endpoints and apex track. Slide the apex from (2,6) through (8,6) to (12,6); a dashed perpendicular to the base line always measures 6. Duplicate a triangle, rotate the duplicate 180 degrees and pair it across a slanted side to form a parallelogram. Its base is 10 and height 6, so each of the two congruent triangles has area 30.
visual: The apex is the only moving vertex. The altitude foot may move outside the base segment, but the extended base line and right-angle marker remain. The duplicate is identified as a second copy, not newly created area inside the first triangle.
transfer_question: Base 8, perpendicular height 5; the apex moves horizontally. Area?
guardrail: Height is the perpendicular distance to the base line, even when the foot falls outside the base segment. This is not a claim about equal perimeter.
why_selected: Strong continuous visual transformation with an invariant the viewer can follow.
alternate_angle: Which two measurements actually control the area?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled stable-apparatus parameter changes and equivalent representations. No equal-area-apex winner was directly reviewed.
revision_reason: Makes the strongest boundary case visible: the altitude falls outside the base, while perpendicular height still controls area.
main_question: A triangle has base 10 and perpendicular height 6. Its apex slides horizontally along y=6. What is its area?
recognition_cue: For triangle area, measure perpendicular height to the base line, not a slanted side.
output_rejection: The apex track tilts, a slanted side is labeled height, or the duplicate does not make a valid parallelogram.

title: Why 8% of 25 is the easy way around
hook: Eight percent of twenty-five. Try twenty-five percent of eight.
first_frame: 8% of 25 = ? beside 25% of 8 = 2. A small equality question connects them; no unexplained instant answer.
prior_knowledge: Percent means per hundred; multiplication is commutative; 25% is one quarter.
promise: Understand when swapping a percent and its quantity preserves the result.
proof_sequence: Establish the swap on an easy 10-by-10 grid of 100 unit cells: the intersection of 20% of the columns and 50% of the rows covers 10 cells in either reading. Then write a% of b = (a/100)b = ab/100 = (b/100)a. Apply to 8% of 25: one quarter of 8 is 2.
answer: 2; a% of b = b% of a because both equal ab/100.
visual: The same 10 cells stay blue as the row/column reading switches. The grid demonstrates 20% of 50, not 8% of 25; make that transition explicit before applying the general algebra to the opening numbers.
transfer_question: Find 4% of 75 using the same swap.
guardrail: This identity concerns numerical percent-of calculations. It does not swap the roles of original and final amounts in percent change, or convert 8% of 25 into 25% more than 8. The grid is one example; algebra supplies generality.
why_selected: The surprising shortcut has a countable rectangle and a one-line general reason, with very low algebra prerequisites.
alternate_angle: One overlap. Two ways to read it.
evidence_scope: New SAT construction using reviewed same-object/two-readings and reference-whole analogues. Percent commutativity itself was not directly reviewed in a reference winner.
revision_reason: New brief: provides a positive structural shortcut, balancing the slate’s error-repair stories.
main_question: Find 8% of 25, and explain why it equals 25% of 8.
recognition_cue: A single percent-of product can be swapped when the other percentage is easier to compute.
output_rejection: The grid is falsely labeled as the opening 8%-by-25 example, or the numerical swap is generalized to reversing a discount.

title: The circle equation is a right triangle
hook: Move this point anywhere on the circle. Which length refuses to change?
first_frame: Center (3,-2), a point (3,5), and a radius labeled 7 on one coordinate plane. Equation: (x-3)²+(y+2)²=49.
prior_knowledge: Pythagoras and distance on perpendicular axes.
promise: Read a circle’s equation as fixed-distance geometry.
proof_sequence: Start at (3,5): its vertical distance from (3,-2) is 7. Move the point to a non-axis location on the same circle and attach a right triangle. The signed coordinate differences are x-3 and y+2; their magnitudes are the leg lengths. Pythagoras gives (x-3)²+(y+2)²=r²=49. Read center (3,-2), radius 7. The equation means all points at that distance.
visual: One fixed center and one tracing point. Horizontal/vertical guides change as the radius stays fixed. Signed coordinate differences appear in the equation; leg labels use absolute values when necessary.
transfer_question: (x + 1)² + (y - 4)² = 36: center and radius?
guardrail: Signed coordinate gaps may be negative but their squares give squared lengths. Radius is nonnegative; 49 is not the radius.
why_selected: A memorized equation becomes familiar geometry, with a concrete SAT payoff.
alternate_angle: Why do two squares describe a circle?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from reviewed circle emergence under constraints and coordinate-frame representations. No source circle-equation lesson was reviewed.
revision_reason: Starts with a visible invariant before asking the equation to carry the explanation; distinguishes signed differences from physical lengths.
main_question: For (x-3)²+(y+2)²=49, find the center and radius.
recognition_cue: A sum of squared coordinate gaps equal to a positive constant describes fixed distance from a center.
output_rejection: A signed gap is silently used as a negative physical length, the center moves, or 49 is called the radius.

title: Three times around. Nine times inside.
hook: Triple a square’s side. Why do its boundary and inside grow differently?
first_frame: A side-2 square sits inside a side-6 outline at the same scale. Readouts: perimeter ×?; area ×?.
prior_knowledge: Area as unit squares, multiplication, and triangle area as half base times perpendicular height.
promise: Distinguish one-dimensional boundary growth from two-dimensional area growth.
proof_sequence: The original perimeter is 8 and area is 4. On the larger boundary, each side contains three original side lengths, giving perimeter 24, or ×3. Fill the larger interior with a 3-by-3 array of original squares, giving area 36, or ×9. Generalize for a square: P=4s scales by k; A=s² scales by k².
visual: First trace the boundary with a single length unit. Then tile the interior with the entire original square as the unit. Change the unit visibly rather than mixing perimeter and area counts.
transfer_question: A square has side 4, then side 10. What are the perimeter and area multipliers?
transfer_answer: Perimeter ×(5/2); area ×(25/4). The old/new values are 16 to 40 and 16 to 100.
guardrail: This brief proves the square case and names the similar-figure scaling relationship only if its general reason is shown. k>0. Do not claim area scales by k² when only one dimension changes.
why_selected: Countable visual surprise with a reusable dimensional rule.
alternate_angle: How many original squares fit inside the enlarged one?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from reviewed parameter escalation and shape measurements. The dimensional-scaling construction was not directly reviewed in a winning reference.
revision_reason: Adds a meaningful contrast: boundary versus interior use different units and different growth laws, rather than only announcing area ×9.
main_question: A square’s side grows from 2 to 6. What happens to its perimeter and area?
recognition_cue: Count how many independent length dimensions the requested measure multiplies.
output_rejection: The larger square is drawn at an inconsistent scale, a perimeter segment is counted as an area tile, or the transfer multiplier is rounded unnecessarily.

title: Why x - 4 moves the graph right
hook: The square still needs the input one. Which x will give it one now?
first_frame: The old point (1,1) lies on y=x². A new input card reads x-4, with an empty slot for the x that feeds the square the same value 1.
prior_knowledge: Substitution and points as input-output pairs.
promise: Explain horizontal translation through the function’s input.
proof_sequence: The original function sends input 1 to output 1. For the new function, the inner input must still equal 1: x-4=1, so x=5. Match (1,1) to (5,1) along a fixed horizontal guide. Repeat with input 0: x-4=0 gives x=4, so the vertex is (4,0). For every old input u, new x=u+4 feeds the same u into the square: every point shifts right four.
answer: The graph shifts 4 units right; its vertex is (4,0).
visual: An input slot sits beside a single matched pair of points. Preserve output height while the x-coordinate changes. Only after both concrete matches does the complete curve translate.
transfer_question: Where does y = (x + 2)² place the vertex?
guardrail: Explain horizontal input shifts separately from a minus outside the function. The result is not a rule that every minus means right.
why_selected: Resolves a familiar sign paradox with one tracked invariant.
alternate_angle: What input does the function actually receive?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled linked-input/output displays and representation changes. No horizontal-translation reference lesson was reviewed.
revision_reason: Replaces an unexplained whole-curve slide with an explicit input requirement and then a general point mapping.
main_question: How does y=(x-4)² relate to y=x², and where is its vertex?
recognition_cue: To preserve the old output, set the new inner input equal to the old input.
output_rejection: The curve moves before a correspondence is earned, axes move with it, or minus-inside is treated as a mnemonic without its input reason.

title: 6 to 26. The mean moves. The median stays.
hook: One dot runs twenty units right. Which average has to chase it?
first_frame: Five ordered dots at 2,3,4,5,6 on a fixed 0-to-28 line. Separate markers: mean=4, median=4. A ghost endpoint at 26 shows the proposed move.
prior_knowledge: Average as total/count and median as middle-ranked value.
promise: Compare mean and median under one specified outlier change.
proof_sequence: Move only the largest dot from 6 to 26. The total rises by 20 while the count remains five, so the mean rises by 20/5=4, from 4 to 8. Keep the five ordered positions labeled first through fifth: the third observation remains 4, so median remains 4. Confirm the new total is 40 and 40/5=8.
visual: A sum/count readout tracks the moving dot, while a rank bracket stays on the third observation. Never rescale the number line to hide the outlier’s distance.
transfer_question: For 1,2,3,4,5, replace 5 with 15. New mean and median?
guardrail: Do not claim outliers never change medians. The result follows from moving the largest value while preserving count and rank of the middle.
why_selected: A large visible move separates two ideas often memorized together.
alternate_angle: Which average uses every value, and which uses position?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from reviewed one-parameter apparatus and linked readouts. The mean/median outcome was not a reviewed reference topic.
revision_reason: The explanation now isolates quantity from rank and derives the mean change from a conserved count.
main_question: For 2,3,4,5,6, replace 6 by 26. Find the new mean and median.
recognition_cue: Mean uses the total and count; median uses the ordered middle position.
output_rejection: The axis rescales, other data values move, or the lesson claims outliers can never affect a median.

title: “Given blue” redraws the whole
hook: Twelve shapes. But only six are still possible.
first_frame: Twelve labeled shapes: 6 blue (3 triangles,3 circles) and 6 ink (1 triangle,5 circles). Prompt: chosen uniformly; given blue, P(triangle)?
prior_knowledge: Probability as favorable outcomes divided by eligible outcomes.
promise: Identify the eligible sample space in conditional probability.
proof_sequence: Show the original 12 as equally likely choices. Apply the condition: the choice is known to be among the six blue shapes. Keep the excluded ink outlines visible but outside the eligible-group bracket. Among the six eligible shapes, exactly three are triangles. Build numerator and denominator from those actual groups: 3/6=1/2.
visual: The denominator bracket moves from all twelve to the six still possible; the numerator outline contains only their three triangles. Labels and shapes carry meaning alongside color.
transfer_question: Choose uniformly among shapes. There are 8 blue shapes, including 2 triangles. Given blue, probability of triangle?
guardrail: Selection is uniform among the eligible shapes. Do not use 3/12 after conditioning, and do not imply the excluded objects disappeared from the original set.
why_selected: One word visibly changes the whole fraction; useful with low algebra prerequisites.
alternate_angle: Which objects are still possible after the condition?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled verification of all 16 membership cases in a replacement four-set diagram. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified. No directly reviewed conditional-probability winner supports the specific hook.
revision_reason: Makes the changed eligible whole an actual bracket operation, while preserving the original population for comparison.
main_question: A shape is chosen uniformly from these 12. Given that it is blue, what is the probability it is a triangle?
recognition_cue: Apply the condition first, then count favorable outcomes within the remaining possible group.
output_rejection: The condition is omitted, selection is not uniform, or the denominator remains twelve after the blue condition.

title: 60 out. 40 back. The average is 48.
hook: Same road. Sixty miles an hour out, forty back. Average fifty?
first_frame: Two equal 120-mile route segments, each labeled with its speed: 60 mph out; 40 mph back. Below, a shared time strip waits to fill.
prior_knowledge: Speed = distance/time and adding durations.
promise: Compute average speed from total distance and total time.
proof_sequence: Run the first equal-distance trip against a clock: 120/60=2 hours. Run the return: 120/40=3 hours. Keep both route lengths equal and concatenate the two time strips. Total distance is 240 miles; total time is 5 hours. Divide: 48 mph. The slower speed receives more time, so an unweighted average of speeds is wrong here.
visual: The trip lengths remain fixed. Only the durations differ. Combine distance with distance and time with time before displaying a rate.
transfer_question: 60 miles at 60 mph, then the same 60 miles at 30 mph. Average speed?
guardrail: Equal distances are essential. Equal time at each speed would give the arithmetic mean; do not generalize the 48 result to that case.
why_selected: A familiar guess fails because time was missing, and units supply the proof.
alternate_angle: Why do the two speeds get unequal weight?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled hidden-quantity accounting and linked quantities. No reviewed reference establishes this travel-speed construction.
revision_reason: Adds a synchronized clock/time-strip construction so the missing denominator is visible before calculation.
main_question: Travel 120 miles at 60 mph and return the same 120 miles at 40 mph. What is the average speed for the full trip?
recognition_cue: Average speed is total distance divided by total elapsed travel time; first determine the time weights.
output_rejection: The routes accidentally have unequal lengths, clocks are absent, or 48 mph is generalized to equal-time trips.

title: Two candidates. One survives the original equation.
hook: Squaring makes two candidates. The original equation accepts only one.
first_frame: The unchanged equation √(x+6)=x sits above two blank candidate slots. A small nonnegative-output marker is attached to the square root.
prior_knowledge: Squaring, factoring, and substitution.
promise: Understand why squared equations require checking candidates.
proof_sequence: The original equation requires x≥0 because its left side is nonnegative. Square to obtain x+6=x² and factor (x-3)(x+2)=0. Bring both algebraic candidates back to the original: 3 gives √9=3; -2 gives √4=2, not -2. Keep only 3. Explain that squaring identifies opposite signs and can therefore admit a candidate the original rejects.
visual: Both candidates return to the same fixed equation. Each side is evaluated separately; the failed equality retains its two different values. This is a candidate-checking construction, not an area animation.
transfer_question: Solve √(x + 2) = x.
guardrail: The principal square root is nonnegative. Squaring may add solutions but does not make both candidates solutions of the original.
why_selected: A clear elimination story tied to an operation’s lost information.
alternate_angle: What information did squaring erase?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from reviewed construction of a replacement four-set diagram and verification of all 16 membership cases. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified. No radical-equation reference was directly reviewed.
revision_reason: Adds the nonnegative-output condition before squaring and makes the failed original equality explicit.
main_question: Solve √(x+6)=x over the real numbers.
recognition_cue: After a step that can lose sign information, verify candidates in the original equation.
output_rejection: The squared equation is called equivalent without its sign condition, or -2 is called a solution before being checked.

title: Count the outcomes you do not want
hook: At least one six. Count the no-sixes instead.
first_frame: A 6-by-6 table of ordered outcomes for two fair independent six-sided dice; row/column labels 1 through 6. Prompt: P(at least one 6)?
prior_knowledge: Probability as favorable equally likely outcomes divided by all outcomes, multiplication and subtracting a complement.
promise: Use the complement to avoid missing or double-counting cases.
proof_sequence: All 36 ordered pairs are equally likely. The no-six outcomes form the upper-left 5-by-5 block, so there are 25. The remaining L-shaped border has 36-25=11 outcomes. Count it a second way: six in the last row plus five more in the last column; (6,6) appears once. Probability is 11/36.
visual: Keep the whole 36-cell table fixed. Outline the 25-cell complement, then reveal the remaining border in blue. The shared corner receives one outline, preventing a misleading 6+6 count.
transfer_question: For the same two dice, what is the probability at least one die shows 5 or 6?
guardrail: Dice are fair and independent, and ordered pairs are the sample space. This is not a condition that a six was observed, and “at least one” includes two sixes.
why_selected: A concrete all-cases picture makes both complement reasoning and the usual double-counting error inspectable.
alternate_angle: Why six plus six is one too many.
evidence_scope: New construction adapted from sampled verification of all 16 membership cases in a replacement four-set diagram, plus whole-minus-part reasoning. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified. No dice winner was directly reviewed.
revision_reason: New brief: adds complement counting with a visibly shared corner, distinct from changing the conditional denominator.
main_question: Roll two fair independent six-sided dice. What is the probability of at least one six?
recognition_cue: For at least one, consider counting none and subtracting from the full set.
output_rejection: The (6,6) corner is counted twice, the sample space treats sums as equally likely, or independence is missing.

title: Why dividing by a negative flips the sign
hook: Multiply both points by minus three. Watch their order reverse.
first_frame: Two labeled points, -5 and -4, on a fixed number line. The inequality -5<-4 is visible above; the operation ×(-3) waits below.
prior_knowledge: Order on a number line and multiplication by negative numbers.
promise: Explain the inequality reversal as a change in order.
proof_sequence: Map each original value t to -3t on a second number line with the same horizontal orientation: -5 maps to 15, -4 to 12. The initially smaller input has the larger output. Generally, if a<b and m<0, then b-a>0 while m(b-a)<0, so mb<ma: multiplication by any negative reverses order. Division by -3 is multiplication by -1/3, so -3x>12 gives x<-4. Check x=-5 passes and x=-3 fails.
visual: Use two aligned number lines rather than relabeling a line under fixed points. Explicit connector guides preserve each point’s identity during reflection and scaling. Finish with an open endpoint at -4.
transfer_question: Solve -2x <= 8.
guardrail: The sign reverses when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative, not when adding a negative. Preserve open/closed endpoint meaning.
why_selected: A memorized rule becomes visible order reversal.
alternate_angle: What happens to left and right when the number line reflects?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled reference-frame changes and tracked correspondences; no reviewed negative-inequality lesson.
revision_reason: Separates the concrete example from the general order argument, so a two-point demonstration does not masquerade as universal proof.
main_question: Solve -3x>12 and explain why the inequality reverses.
recognition_cue: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative reverses order; adding a negative does not.
output_rejection: A single checked pair is called a general proof, the mapping changes only one side, or the endpoint becomes closed.

title: One step bigger needs forty-one tiles
hook: Twenty squared to twenty-one squared. Why do you add forty-one?
first_frame: A 20-by-20 square inside a 21-by-21 outline. One-unit strips along the top and right are visibly unfilled; difference = ?.
prior_knowledge: Square area, unit-square counting and distributing a product.
promise: See why consecutive square areas differ by the next odd number.
proof_sequence: Keep the 20-by-20 region fixed. Add a 20-by-1 top strip and a 20-by-1 right strip, then the separate 1-by-1 corner. The added area is 20+20+1=41. Replace 20 by n: (n+1)²-n²=2n+1 by the same nondegenerate partition for n>0; distributivity proves the identity for every real n.
visual: The two thin strips and corner are separate labeled regions. Do not render 400 tiny cells: use boundary ticks and dimensions so the added 20+20+1 is legible.
transfer_question: Find 100²-99² without computing both squares.
guardrail: The nondegenerate positive-length picture uses n>0; n=0 is a degenerate boundary case. Calling the difference an odd integer additionally requires integer n. Do not double-count the corner or infer the identity from only a list of observed differences.
why_selected: A growing parameter supplies an escalating pattern while the geometric partition proves it.
alternate_angle: Where do the odd numbers live in a square?

title: Two unknowns. One fixed answer.
hook: a and b can move. Why does this answer stay sixteen?
first_frame: Constraint 3a+2b=4 above linked a,b readouts, initially a=0,b=2. Target: 8ᵃ·4ᵇ = ?.
prior_knowledge: Powers, powers of powers, and multiplying equal bases.
promise: Recognize a given expression inside combined exponents.
proof_sequence: Show three permitted pairs: (0,2),(1,1/2),(2,-1). The target evaluates to 16 each time, suggesting an invariant rather than proving it. Rewrite 8ᵃ·4ᵇ=(2³)ᵃ(2²)ᵇ=2^(3a+2b). The fixed exponent is 4, so the expression is always 16 for every permitted pair.
visual: A single constraint links the readouts; b updates as (4-3a)/2 when a moves. After the numerical cases, align the entire combined exponent directly under the given 3a+2b. Keep fractional/negative inputs labeled.
transfer_question: If 2p + q = 5, find 4ᵖ × 2ᑫ.
guardrail: The product uses positive bases; no numerical values for a or b are determined or needed.
why_selected: A scary expression collapses through one visible structural match.
alternate_angle: Why do two unknowns still give one definite answer?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled surprising emergence under constraints and one-parameter escalation. The exponent construction was not directly reviewed.
revision_reason: Turns the symbolic match into a constrained changing system, then explicitly distinguishes repeated examples from the general algebraic reason.
main_question: For real a,b with 3a+2b=4, find 8ᵃ·4ᵇ.
recognition_cue: Rewrite powers with a common positive base and look for the given combination inside the exponent.
output_rejection: Three examples are called a proof, the readouts violate 3a+2b=4, or positive bases are replaced by unrestricted negative-base powers.

title: When matching coefficients makes a contradiction
hook: Make the left sides identical. The right sides still disagree.
first_frame: 2x+ky=6 and 4x+6y=15 above two graph lines at k=2. A single k control shows the target: no solution.
prior_knowledge: Equivalent equations, line slope, and contradiction.
promise: Distinguish parallel distinct lines from the same line.
proof_sequence: Double the first equation: 4x+2ky=12. Subtract it from the second: (6-2k)y=3. For k=3, the left side is 0 for every y, giving 0=3: no solution. For k≠3, y=3/(6-2k) is unique and the first equation determines one x, so no other k works. At k=3, hold the two distinct parallel lines as geometric confirmation.
visual: Vary k only near 2 to 4, with an explicit pause at 3. Match coefficient columns above the graph. Do not follow a crossing toward infinity or use its disappearance as the proof.
transfer_question: 2x + ky = 6 and 4x + 8y = 15: no-solution k?
guardrail: A crossing leaving the screen does not prove no solution. If the constants were also proportional, the lines would coincide instead.
why_selected: A dramatic geometric endpoint paired with an exact algebraic reason.
alternate_angle: What turns a crossing into a contradiction?
evidence_scope: Adaptation from sampled parameter change and representations of the same structure. This no-solution construction was not directly reviewed.
revision_reason: Moves the exact contradiction to center stage and proves uniqueness of the exceptional parameter, rather than relying on an off-screen intersection.
main_question: Which real k makes 2x+ky=6 and 4x+6y=15 have no solution?
recognition_cue: Proportional variable coefficients with incompatible constants give distinct parallel lines.
output_rejection: An intersection leaving the viewport is the only reason, or proportional constants are mistakenly called no solution.

title: One height. Two inputs.
hook: This height hits the parabola twice. Keep both inputs.
first_frame: A readable graph of y=(x-3)² and the horizontal line y=4, with two crossing points visible but x labels hidden. Prompt: (x-3)²=4.
prior_knowledge: Squares, signed numbers, graph intersections as equal outputs and horizontal shifts.
promise: Connect the two square-root branches to two actual input values.
proof_sequence: The distance of x from 3 must be 2, so mark the two x positions 3-2 and 3+2. Algebraically, x-3=2 or x-3=-2, hence x=5 or x=1. Label the same two graph crossings and substitute each into the original. Contrast the equation with evaluating √4, which has the single principal value 2.
visual: Keep the symmetry line x=3 and y=4 fixed. Two horizontal distance brackets of length 2 connect the vertex’s x-coordinate to the two solutions. The brackets measure x-distance, not the slanted distance along the curve.
transfer_question: Solve (x+2)²=9 over the real numbers.
guardrail: The squared quantity has two possible signs when the right side is positive. √4 itself is 2, never ±2. At right side 0 there is one real solution; at a negative right side there are none over the reals.
why_selected: A bounded two-input story earns both algebraic branches and strengthens a foundational SAT recognition cue.
alternate_angle: A square remembers the distance but forgets the side.
evidence_scope: New construction adapted from sampled linked representations and verification of all 16 membership cases in a replacement four-set diagram. The original diagram's specific missing case was not explicitly identified. No quadratic-root reference was directly reviewed.
revision_reason: Replaces the prior isolated principal-root example with two actual intersections and an explicit distinction between evaluation and solving.
main_question: Solve (x-3)²=4 over the real numbers.
recognition_cue: When a squared expression equals a positive number, retain both signs before isolating x.
output_rejection: The graph has only one crossing, the minus branch disappears, √4 is written ±2, or horizontal distances are confused with curve lengths.
